# Diagnosing Air Bleed from the Carburetor on a Briggs & Stratton 33R877

A Briggs & Stratton 33R877 engine blowing air out of the carburetor during the compression stroke, specifically after top dead center (TDC), points to a specific mechanical failure rather than a simple timing misalignment. When you manually rotate the crankshaft and feel resistance that coincides with air being sucked in and then pushed back out through the intake path, the engine is effectively bypassing its compression seal. This behavior indicates that one of the valves is failing to close at the precise moment required to trap the air-fuel mixture.

The symptom describedâdifficulty turning the crankshaft starting around 25 degrees before TDC and persisting past itâis the classic signature of an open intake valve. If the inlet valve remains open while the piston rises, high-pressure combustion gases or fresh charge will escape back into the carburetor manifold. This creates a "free-wheeling" effect where the engine loses compression, making the starter motor work harder than usual because it is trying to compress nothing but moving against friction and internal leakage.

You have already verified that the camshaft and crankshaft alignment dots match, and you confirmed the rocker arm pusher rods are in place with the correct materials (steel for exhaust, aluminum for intake). However, verifying gear alignment does not guarantee valve timing accuracy if the lifters or the rocker arms themselves have shifted position. On OHV engines like the 33R877, the camshaft drives a tappet that pushes directly on the rocker arm shaft or individual rocker arms depending on the specific sub-model year.

The most likely culprit is incorrect valve lash adjustment or a damaged rocker arm mechanism. Even if the gears are lined up, if the pusher rods (rocker arms) were installed without setting the proper clearance, the intake valve may be hitting the seat too hard and rebounding open, or it may not be seating fully. A common mistake during reassembly is failing to set the "cold" lash before thermal expansion occurs. If you tightened the adjustment nuts on the rocker arm shafts immediately after assembly, the engine will expand as it warms up, taking up the slack and potentially opening the valve prematurely or preventing a full seal.

Another possibility involves the valve guides or the valve stems themselves. If the intake valve stem is bent even slightly, or if the guide is worn, the valve may tilt when pushed down by the cam lobe, failing to close completely against the seat. This physical misalignment would persist regardless of gear timing. Additionally, inspect the valve spring retainer and lock washers is critical; a broken lock washer can allow the spring to collapse, losing all tension and allowing the valve to float open during compression.

Before tearing down the rocker box again, try this diagnostic step: remove the spark plug and crank the engine over by hand while watching the valves through the spark hole (if accessible) or using an inspection mirror. Observe the intake valve at TDC. If you see it lifting off its seat when the piston is attempting to compress, the issue is confirmed as a mechanical failure in the rocker arm assembly or the pusher rod linkage.

If the pusher rods are indeed mixed up (aluminum vs. steel), ensure they match the manufacturer's specification exactly. Using the wrong material can lead to wear patterns that alter the effective length of the lever, changing the valve lift profile. Sometimes, a worn bushing in the rocker arm shaft can allow the arm to pivot out of its intended plane, effectively camming the valve open under load.

If these checks do not resolve the issue, you may need to inspect the cylinder head gasket seating surface or the combustion chamber for warping. However, given the specific description of air escaping only after compression starts, the fault lies almost exclusively in the intake valve's ability to maintain a seal under pressure. Ensure all new gaskets are seated perfectly flat and that no debris is caught between the cylinder head and the block, which could warp the head locally upon heating.
